title: Work, Energy, and Power in Humans
lead: Your own body is an energy conversion machine, and conservation of energy holds for it as it does for a roller coaster. This section follows the chemical energy stored in food as it becomes work done on the outside world, thermal energy, and fat. It gives the rate at which the body spends that energy its name, the metabolic rate, and the value it takes at rest; it shows that the rate can be measured by measuring the oxygen a person breathes; and it says which of the work a person does counts as useful work, and how much food a day of activity costs.
objectives: Explain the human body’s consumption of energy when at rest vs. when engaged in activities that do useful work.
Calculate the conversion of chemical energy in food into useful work.
summary_html:
• The human body converts energy stored in food into work, thermal energy, and/or chemical energy that is stored in fatty tissue.
  • The rate at which the body uses food energy to sustain life and to do different activities is called the metabolic rate, and the corresponding rate when at rest is called the basal metabolic rate (BMR)
  • The energy included in the basal metabolic rate is divided among various systems in the body, with the largest fraction going to the liver and spleen, and the brain coming next.
  • About 75% of food calories are used to sustain basic body functions included in the basal metabolic rate.
  • The energy consumption of people during various activities can be determined by measuring their oxygen use, because the digestive process is basically one of oxidizing food.
notes: The sprinter’s power output, the out-of-condition person’s efficiency, the daily energy need read off Table 7.5, the shovelling of snow, the jogger’s leg, the flight of the Daedalus 88, the mountain climber’s bottled oxygen and the candy bar are the section’s unkeyed problems, and all eight are left out; the book’s photograph of the Daedalus 88 belonged to one of them and is not copied.

figures.original_caption: Energy consumed by humans is converted to work, thermal energy, and stored fat. By far the largest fraction goes to thermal energy, although the fraction varies depending on the type of physical activity.

exercises.prompt: Explain why it is easier to climb a mountain on a zigzag path rather than one straight up the side. Is your increase in gravitational potential energy the same in both cases? Is your energy consumption the same in both?

answer.solution: The zigzag path is longer, but it rises at a gentler angle, so at every step the part of your weight you must work against along the path is smaller and your legs need to exert less force at any moment. The increase in gravitational potential energy is the same on both paths, because it is $m\kg\kh$ and depends only on the height you gain, and gravity is a conservative force, so the route makes no difference to it. Your energy consumption is not the same. The zigzag takes longer, and your body spends food energy at its metabolic rate for the whole of that time; on either path most of what you metabolise becomes thermal energy and goes into lifting and lowering your own legs rather than into the potential energy of your centre of mass. The zigzag is easier because it asks for less force at any one moment, not because it asks for less energy, and it generally asks for somewhat more.

exercises.prompt: Do you do work on the outside world when you rub your hands together to warm them? What is the efficiency of this activity?

answer.solution: You do no useful work. Each hand presses on the other and slides, and both hands are part of you, so no force you exert moves anything in the outside world through a distance. The work your muscles do goes into the friction between your palms and becomes thermal energy, which is the whole point of rubbing them. Since useful work is work done on the outside world, the useful work output is zero, and the efficiency, which is the useful work divided by the food energy metabolised to do it, is zero as well. That is not a failure here: warming your hands is a case where the thermal energy is what you are after, so an efficiency of zero is exactly what you want.

exercises.prompt: Shivering is an involuntary response to lowered body temperature. What is the efficiency of the body when shivering, and is this a desirable value?

answer.solution: Shivering pits muscles against one another, so the forces they exert act on other parts of your own body and nothing outside you is moved through a distance. The useful work output is zero, and so the efficiency of the body while shivering is zero. Here that is the value you want. Shivering is an involuntary response to a low body temperature, and its purpose is to turn food energy into thermal energy inside the body as quickly as it can; any energy that left as useful work would be energy that did not warm you. Table 7.5 shows how much energy that takes: shivering consumes 425 W, about three and a half times the rate of sitting at rest.

exercises.prompt: Discuss the relative impact of dieting and exercise, noting that most athletic activities consume food energy at a rate of 400 to 500 W, while a single cup of yogurt can contain 1360 kJ (325 kcal).

answer.solution: Compare the two as rates. A cup of yogurt holds 1360 kJ, and an activity that consumes food energy at 450 W works that much off in about 3000 s, which is roughly fifty minutes of steady exercise for one cup. Choosing not to eat the yogurt takes no time at all, so as a way of changing the balance between the energy eaten and the energy spent, dieting acts far faster than exercise. Example 7.13 makes the same point from the other side: a surplus of only 1000 kJ, which is less than a tenth of a day’s food energy, takes 42 minutes of cycling to work off. Exercise still matters, because it raises the rate at which the body spends energy while it lasts, because muscle mass burns more calories than body fat and so raises the basal metabolic rate, and because it does the body good in ways that eating less does not. But the arithmetic says that someone who wants to lose fat will find it easier to eat less than to exercise the same amount away.

exercises.prompt: (a) How long can you rapidly climb stairs (116/min) on the 93.0 kcal of energy in a 10.0-g pat of butter? (b) How many flights is this if each flight has 16 stairs?

parts.hint: Table 7.5 gives 685 W for climbing stairs at 116 a minute, and one food calorie is 4186 J, so the time is the food energy divided by that rate.
At 116 stairs a minute for the time you found in (a), count the stairs and divide by the 16 in a flight.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the power output in watts and horsepower of a shot-putter who takes 1.20 s to accelerate the 7.27-kg shot from rest to 14.0 m/s, while raising it 0.800 m. (Do not include the power produced to accelerate his body.)

parts.hint: The useful work is the kinetic energy the shot is given plus the potential energy of raising it 0.800 m, and the power is that work divided by 1.20 s.

exercises.prompt: Energy that is not utilized for work or heat transfer is converted to the chemical energy of body fat containing about 39 kJ/g. How many grams of fat will you gain if you eat 10,000 kJ (about 2500 kcal) one day and do nothing but sit relaxed for 16.0 h and sleep for the other 8.00 h? Use data from Table 7.5 for the energy consumption rates of these activities.

answer.hint: Table 7.5 gives 120 W for sitting at rest and 83 W for sleeping. Find the energy the day costs, subtract it from the 10,000 kJ you ate, and divide what is left over by the 39 kJ that go into each gram of fat.

exercises.prompt: What is the efficiency of a subject on a treadmill who puts out work at the rate of 100 W while consuming oxygen at the rate of 2.00 L/min? (Hint: See Table 7.5.)

answer.hint: About 20 kJ of energy is produced for each litre of oxygen consumed, so 2.00 L/min is a rate of food energy in watts; the efficiency is the 100 W of useful work divided by that rate.

exercises.prompt: Very large forces are produced in joints when a person jumps from some height to the ground. (a) Calculate the magnitude of the force produced if an 80.0-kg person jumps from a 0.600–m-high ledge and lands stiffly, compressing joint material 1.50 cm as a result. (Be certain to include the weight of the person.) (b) In practice the knees bend almost involuntarily to help extend the distance over which you stop. Calculate the magnitude of the force produced if the stopping distance is 0.300 m. (c) Compare both forces with the weight of the person.

parts.hint: The person keeps falling while the joint material compresses, so the gravitational potential energy lost over the whole descent, the ledge plus the 1.50 cm, becomes the work the stopping force does through 1.50 cm.
Run the same energy account with a stopping distance of 0.300 m in place of 1.50 cm and see how much smaller the force becomes.

answer.solution: (a) $3.21\times 10^{4}\ \text{N}$ (b) $2.35\times 10^{3}\ \text{N}$ (c) The ratio of the net force to the weight of the person is 41.0 in part (a) and 3.00 in part (b).

exercises.prompt: (a) Calculate the energy in kJ used by a 55.0-kg person who does 50 deep knee bends in which their center of mass is lowered and raised 0.400 m. (They do work in both directions.) You may assume their efficiency is 20%. (b) What is the average power consumption rate in watts if they do this in 3.00 min?

parts.hint: Each bend lowers and raises the centre of mass by 0.400 m and work is done in both directions, so the useful work is fifty times twice $m\kg\kh$; the food energy is that work divided by the efficiency of 20%.
Divide the food energy by 3.00 min written in seconds.

The arm action is shown by an arc starting from where his hand enters the surface of the water and ending at the point where his hand emerges from the water. The diameter of this arc made by the person’s hand tip in one stroke is one point eight meters.

exercises.prompt: The swimmer shown in the figure exerts an average horizontal backward force of 80.0 N with his arm during each 1.80 m long stroke. (a) What is his work output in each stroke? (b) Calculate the power output of his arms if he does 120 strokes per minute.

parts.hint: The force is along the stroke, so the work is $\kW = \kF\kd$ over the 1.80 m of one stroke.
120 strokes a minute is two strokes a second, so the power is the work of one stroke multiplied by that rate.

exercises.prompt: The awe-inspiring Great Pyramid of Cheops was built more than 4500 years ago. Its square base, originally 230 m on a side, covered 13.1 acres, and it was 146 m high, with a mass of about $7\times {10}^{9}\;\text{kg}$. (The pyramid’s dimensions are slightly different today due to quarrying and some sagging.) Historians estimate that 20,000 workers spent 20 years to construct it, working 12-hour days, 330 days per year. (a) Calculate the gravitational potential energy stored in the pyramid, given its center of mass is at one-fourth its height. (b) Only a fraction of the workers lifted blocks; most were involved in support services such as building ramps (see the figure), bringing food and water, and hauling blocks to the site. Calculate the efficiency of the workers who did the lifting, assuming there were 1000 of them and they consumed food energy at the rate of 300 kcal/h. What does your answer imply about how much of their work went into block-lifting, versus how much work went into friction and lifting and lowering their own bodies? (c) Calculate the mass of food that had to be supplied each day, assuming that the average worker required 3600 kcal per day and that their diet was 5% protein, 60% carbohydrate, and 35% fat. (These proportions neglect the mass of bulk and nondigestible materials consumed.)

parts.hint: The centre of mass is at one fourth of the 146 m, so the potential energy is $m\kg\kh$ with that height.
Work out the food energy the 1000 lifters metabolised over 20 years of 330 twelve-hour days at 300 kcal an hour, and divide the potential energy of the pyramid by it.
Find the energy each gram of protein, carbohydrate and fat supplies, take the mixture in the stated proportions, and scale to 3600 kcal a day for each of the 20,000 workers.
